clue.text: Poor Edward, interrupted by female and made to look small

indicators.note: something interrupted is broken into, so the shuffled name is split open to take a letter
poor here means in bad shape, so the name's letters are knocked into a new order

explanation.surface: Poor Edward is made to feel tiny when a woman cuts in on him.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Poor' turns EDWARD into DWARED, and 'interrupted by' puts F inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: To be overshadowed by something far bigger is to look small beside it.

clue.text: Note on side indicating to lift lid

parts.note: D is a musical note
the off side is one half of a cricket field

explanation.surface: A memo about which side shows the way to raise a cover.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lid' is slang for a hat; the off side in cricket is the half of the field the batsman faces.
explanation.definitionFit: Raising a hat in greeting is taking it off, and lid is slang for headwear.

clue.text: Accommodation for schools on display

parts.note: schools here are shoals of fish, housed in glass tanks for viewing

explanation.definitionFit: Glass tanks or buildings where fish are kept for public viewing.

clue.text: Integrated with a safety device

definitions.meaning: fitted with a fuse, which breaks a circuit when overloaded

explanation.definitionFit: Joined into a single whole; also fitted with a protective electrical cut-out.

clue.text: One can get hammered on wicket that has no life in it

definitions.text: One can get hammered on wicket
definitions.meaning: a wicket is a small door or gate, onto which a nail may be hammered

definitions.text: that has no life in it
definitions.meaning: the saying 'dead as a ...' uses this as its image of lifelessness

explanation.walkthrough: 'Wicket' suggests cricket, but here it is a small gate or door.
explanation.definitionFit: A nail driven into a door; and the stock simile for something utterly dead.

clue.text: Space for horses cut by a foot

parts.note: an animal's pad is its foot
to dock a tail is to cut it short

explanation.surface: A horse enclosure trimmed by twelve inches.
explanation.definitionFit: An enclosed field where horses graze or are kept before a race.

clue.text: Like to give satisfaction

definitions.meaning: as in 'do as you like', meaning to wish

explanation.definitionFit: Choose as you wish; also to make someone content.

clue.text: Does Harry set out to become a fine puller of beer?

indicators.note: set out means arranged afresh, so these letters are put in a new order

explanation.surface: Harry sets out to become an expert barman.
explanation.walkthrough: 'puller of beer' looks like a barman, but it is a horse pulling a brewer's cart.
explanation.definitionFit: A strong horse used to haul a brewer's cart laden with barrels.

clue.text: Systematic study of listeners' complaints

parts.note: listeners are ears, so this is the medical science of ear disorders, not of grumbling audiences

explanation.definitionFit: The branch of medicine dealing with the ear and its diseases.

clue.text: End of a line — monarch's upset

parts.note: a king is a monarch, here possessive
cross means annoyed or upset

explanation.surface: At the end of the line, the monarch is upset.
explanation.walkthrough: KING'S CROSS is a major London railway terminus, where lines end.
explanation.definitionFit: A London rail terminus where the East Coast main line terminates.

clue.text: Side all out with seven ducks, making eighty?

definitions.text: Side all out with seven ducks, making eighty?

parts.words: Side all out with seven ducks, making eighty?
parts.note: a cricket team of eleven is dismissed with seven players making nothing, so only a quartet got runs; that reading also names an old way of saying eighty (four twenties)

explanation.walkthrough: In cricket a duck is a score of nothing; seven ducks in a side of eleven leaves four who scored.
explanation.definitionFit: Score is an old word for twenty, so four twenties make eighty.

clue.text: Trouble afoot? It could grow considerably

definitions.meaning: read as two words, a sore patch of hard skin on the toe is trouble on the foot
a small oak nut can grow into a huge tree

explanation.walkthrough: 'Afoot' usually means under way; here it means literally on the foot.
explanation.definitionFit: An oak's seed is tiny yet becomes a great tree; split in two the word is a painful foot complaint.

clue.text: Sporting establishments taking lots of swimmers from Yorkshire once?

parts.note: Yorkshire was formerly divided into three Ridings, North, East and West
schools are large groups of fish

explanation.surface: Sports clubs recruit big shoals of fish out of an old English county.
explanation.walkthrough: Yorkshire is a large county in northern England whose old divisions were called Ridings.
explanation.definitionFit: Places that teach horsemanship are establishments devoted to an equestrian sport.

clue.text: Boastful buffoon ruined a car so much

indicators.note: ruined means wrecked, so the letters are broken up and rebuilt

explanation.surface: A braggart clown wrecks his car badly.
explanation.definitionFit: A stock character of Italian comedy, a cowardly braggart and clown.

clue.text: Man who does army service sounds like a Charlie

indicators.note: the clue says the definition is pronounced like the name that follows

parts.note: Charlie Chaplin was the famous silent-film comedian

explanation.surface: A soldier who seems to resemble a fool.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Charlie' is British slang for a fool, but here it points to the comic film star; 'service' is a church service, not military duty.
explanation.definitionFit: A clergyman attached to a regiment leads its religious services.

clue.text: Gift from sweetheart means nothing to Scotsman

parts.note: love means nil in tennis scoring
taken as written
Ken, short for Kenneth, is a typically Scottish man's name

explanation.surface: A present from a lover means nothing to a man from Scotland.
explanation.definitionFit: A keepsake given as a sign of affection.

clue.text: Possibly collect rupees held by settler

indicators.note: held by means kept inside, so one piece sits within the other

parts.note: someone who settles a bill is the payer
R is the abbreviation for rupees, the Indian currency

explanation.surface: Someone settling accounts holds onto the money they gather.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Collect' is not the verb but the noun: a short prayer read in church services.
explanation.definitionFit: A collect is a short liturgical petition to God, one example of the wider kind.

clue.text: Drifting, in the main? Get back on even keel

definitions.meaning: the main is the open sea, where a sailing ship stuck without wind is left idle
read as two words, to become tranquil again

explanation.definitionFit: A sailing ship without wind is stuck at sea; split in two the word means to be soothed.

clue.text: Expel some Greyfriars pupils

definitions.meaning: to expel is to send away or take out
at Greyfriars, Billy Bunter's fictional school, his class was called by this form name

explanation.walkthrough: Greyfriars is the boarding school of Frank Richards's Billy Bunter stories, where Bunter is in this form.
explanation.definitionFit: To expel is to take away; the same word names a school form in the Billy Bunter stories.

clue.text: Forming such insults is child's play

definitions.text: Forming such insults is child's play

parts.words: Forming such insults is child's play
parts.note: insults are mud thrown at someone; shaping wet earth into pretend pastries is what small children do

explanation.definitionFit: Little cakes of wet earth made by children at play.

clue.text: Handsome 'ero in biology group .

indicators.note: in places the dropped-aitch word inside the other piece

parts.note: a genus is a rank in biological classification
the clue's own spelling of hero with a dropped H, taken as written

explanation.surface: A good-looking working-class hero turns up in a biology class.
explanation.definitionFit: A handsome gift or sum is a lavish one, as an open-handed donor gives.

clue.text: Matilda was prone to be on top like this

definitions.text: Matilda was prone to be on top like this

parts.words: Matilda was prone to be on top like this
parts.note: Belloc's Matilda told such dreadful lies, so she lied too much; prone and on top describe lying upon something

explanation.walkthrough: Matilda is from Hilaire Belloc's cautionary verse about a girl who told lies and was burnt to death.
explanation.definitionFit: To lie on top of something; also, split, telling too many falsehoods.

clue.text: Almost pierce with javelin, perhaps, a high-jumper from Africa

indicators.note: almost means not quite all, so the last letter is dropped

parts.note: to impale is to run through with a spike, a javelin being one example

explanation.surface: An athlete nearly spears a high jumper from Africa with a javelin.
explanation.walkthrough: 'javelin' and 'high-jumper' paint athletics; the jumper is an antelope.
explanation.definitionFit: An African antelope famous for its enormous leaps.

clue.text: Fitting for one such as Cinders, say, to go to the dance

definitions.meaning: fitting means tailored precisely, as clothes are

definitions.text: for one such as Cinders, say, to go to the dance
definitions.meaning: Cinderella was compelled, so 'made', to go to a ball, where a measure is a stately dance

explanation.walkthrough: A measure is an old word for a dance; Cinders is Cinderella of the pantomime.
explanation.definitionFit: Clothes tailored to one person's size fit exactly; split up, the phrase says she was compelled to go to a dance.

clue.text: Occupying subordinate position in launderette

indicators.note: in means the letters lie within the word that follows

explanation.surface: Someone works in a junior role at a laundrette.
explanation.definitionFit: Being below in rank, as an underling is.

clue.text: Idiot told off

indicators.note: off means gone wrong, so the letters are put out of order

explanation.definitionFit: A stupid, slow-witted person.

clue.text: Plan to get back into this country in paddle boat

indicators.note: into means the turned word is set inside the other

parts.note: UK, the abbreviation for the United Kingdom, where the paper is printed

indicators.note: get back means the word for plan is read from its end to its start

parts.note: to aim is to plan or intend

explanation.surface: Someone intends to return home in a small rowing boat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'paddle boat' suggests a pedalo, but it is an Inuit craft; 'get back' makes MIA and 'into' sets it in the home country.
explanation.definitionFit: An Inuit open skin boat propelled with paddles.

clue.text: After false alarm I'd look for this well-protected animal

indicators.note: after means the next piece follows the rearranged letters
false means not genuine, so the letters are rearranged into a different word

parts.note: lo is an old word meaning look

explanation.surface: Following a false alarm, someone searches for an armoured creature.
explanation.walkthrough: 'look for this' reads as a search, but 'look' is the old exclamation; 'false' rearranges the two words before it and 'After' puts the exclamation last.
explanation.definitionFit: This South American mammal has a hard bony shell like armour.

clue.text: One way to praise book girl read either way

parts.note: Hos is the abbreviation for the biblical book of Hosea

indicators.note: the name spells the same from front or back, so the clue's way of saying it does not change

parts.note: Anna is a girl's name

explanation.surface: A book about a girl whose name reads the same both ways praises someone.
explanation.definitionFit: A shout of adoration used in worship, especially in hymns.

clue.text: Most ignorant just before it dawns on one

definitions.meaning: being most in the dark means knowing least

definitions.text: just before it dawns on one
definitions.meaning: the saying goes that night is blackest just before dawn; here dawning is realisation

explanation.definitionFit: Being in the dark means ignorance; the proverb puts the blackest hour just before daybreak.
